nghi_van.mo_ta: A tall, plain, dark-grey rectangular slab with no windows or roof detail stands in the middle of the brick rooftops. It looks like a modern concrete or steel block.
nghi_van.ly_do: No windowless monolithic tower block like this existed in 1670 London. It is a modern-looking structure.

tra_loi.vat: A tall, flat-sided dark grey block in the middle of the red-brick houses. It looks like a modern concrete tower or slab.
tra_loi.dac_diem: It is a plain, windowless, rectangular grey-brown slab with a flat top. It has no roof pitch, no chimneys and no visible windows. It is much taller than the surrounding pitched-roof brick houses, and its texture and colour differ from the brick.
tra_loi.ly_do: A tall, featureless concrete-style slab does not match 1670 London, which had low brick and timber houses with pitched roofs. Concrete high-rise blocks only appeared in the 20th century.

ghi_chu.mo_ta: A long, pale cream-white terrace with a uniform row of windows sits on the skyline. It looks like a Georgian or Regency terrace.
ghi_chu.ly_do: Long uniform plastered terraces are an 18th–19th century form. London in 1670 was mostly timber or brick houses with varied gabled frontages.

ghi_chu.mo_ta: The whole district is uniform red-brick houses with regular grids of white-framed sash windows, slate roofs and tall brick chimneys. It reads as a Georgian townscape. There is no Old St Paul's ruin and no medieval church towers in the view.
ghi_chu.ly_do: London in 1670 was still mid-rebuilding after the 1666 Fire. Many houses were timber-framed or jettied, and sash windows were only just appearing. The ruins of Old St Paul's should stand as a landmark, and the view shows no sign of them.
